entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A serious, honest and private conversation, usually between two people who are close, about their feelings or personal problems.
entries.usage: Usually with *have*: *have a heart-to-heart with someone about something*. It suggests trust and emotion, typical between family members, friends or partners, often after a time of tension or before a big decision. It also works before a noun: *a heart-to-heart talk*.
entries.pattern: have a heart-to-heart (with someone) (about something)
examples: After weeks of silence, my dad and I finally had **a heart-to-heart** about why he missed my graduation.
Before the playoffs, the coach sat down with his star player for **a heart-to-heart** about his attitude.
My best friend and I stayed up until two in the morning having **a heart-to-heart** about our marriages.

drill.sentence: Mom could tell something was wrong, so she made us some tea and we had {{a heart-to-heart}} at the kitchen table.
drill.hint: an honest, emotional one-on-one talk (not *a long talk* or *a chat*)

entries.related: *a deep conversation* — plainer; *clear the air* — talk openly to end tension; *a pep talk* — a short talk to encourage someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person or thing that is new, different and pleasantly refreshing, especially after something dull or unpleasant.
entries.usage: Very common praise for people, places, styles and ideas, usually with *be*: *The new teacher is a breath of fresh air.* It almost always implies a contrast with what came before. *It's a breath of fresh air to* + verb is also common, and the literal sense (going outside for some air) still exists.
entries.pattern: be a breath of fresh air / it's a breath of fresh air to + verb
examples: After years of grumpy managers, our new boss is **a breath of fresh air**: she actually says thank you.
In a summer full of sequels, that quirky little indie movie was **a breath of fresh air**.
It's **a breath of fresh air** to find a mechanic who doesn't try to sell me things I don't need.

drill.sentence: The new owners turned the gloomy old diner into a bright, friendly place; it's {{a breath of fresh air}} on our block.
drill.hint: something new and pleasantly different — an outdoor breathing image (not *a welcome change*)

entries.related: *a welcome change* — plainer; *a change of pace* — a pleasant break from routine; *refreshing* — the one-word adjective.

entries.term: pull the wool over someone's eyes
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deceive someone so that they don't see what is really happening.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, very often in the negative or as a warning: *Don't try to pull the wool over my eyes.* *You can't pull the wool over her eyes* praises someone as hard to fool. Only the possessive changes (*my / his / investors' eyes*); the rest of the phrase is fixed.
entries.pattern: pull the wool over someone's eyes
examples: The seller tried to **pull the wool over our eyes** by painting over the water damage on the ceiling.
My grandmother is sharp; you can't **pull the wool over her eyes** about anything.
For years, the company **pulled the wool over** investors' **eyes** with fake sales numbers.

drill.sentence: My son claimed he'd been at the library all evening, but he couldn't {{pull the wool over my eyes}}; his shoes were covered in mud.
drill.hint: fool me — an image of sheep's fleece (not *put one over on me*)

entries.related: *pull a fast one (on someone)* — trick someone, more casual; *take someone for a ride* — cheat or deceive someone; *see through someone* — recognize the deception.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To share the cost of a meal, date or outing, with each person paying their own part.
entries.usage: Informal, mostly about restaurants and dates: *Let's go Dutch.* People use it both for paying for your own order and for splitting the total evenly. *Split the check* is more common in everyday American speech; *Dutch* always has a capital *D*.
entries.pattern: go Dutch / let's go Dutch
examples: On our first date, she insisted that we **go Dutch**, so we each paid for our own pasta.
Some couples **go Dutch** on everything, even after they've moved in together.
"Let me get this." "No, let's **go Dutch**; I ordered way more than you did."

drill.sentence: We're both students on tight budgets, so when we eat out, we always {{go Dutch}}.
drill.hint: each pay our own share — named after a European nation (not *split the check*)

entries.related: *split the check / bill* — divide the total, more common today; *pick up the tab* — pay for everyone; *my treat* — I'm paying.
entries.origin: From the older American phrase *Dutch treat* (late 1800s), an outing where everyone pays for themselves.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get full value for what you paid, so that the price feels fair or even generous.
entries.usage: Common in everyday talk about meals, tickets, trips and memberships: *We really got our money's worth.* It is often humorous when people overuse something because they paid for it: *I stayed until closing to get my money's worth.* The possessive changes (*our / his / their money's worth*); note the apostrophe in *money's*.
entries.pattern: get your money's worth (out of something)
examples: The concert lasted almost four hours, so we definitely **got our money's worth**.
Dad ate four plates at the buffet, determined to **get his money's worth**.
If you're paying for a gym membership, go at least three times a week to **get your money's worth**.

drill.sentence: The ski passes cost a fortune, so we stayed on the slopes from the first lift to the last to {{get our money's worth}}.
drill.hint: receive full value for what we paid (not *make the most of it*)

entries.related: *value for money* — the usual British phrase; *bang for your buck* — informal American, value for the money spent; *a rip-off* — the opposite, far too expensive.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very regularly and predictably, or very smoothly and exactly as planned.
entries.usage: Used after verbs like *run, go, work* and *arrive*: *The wedding went like clockwork.* It covers both regular timing (*The bus comes at 7:10, like clockwork*) and smooth organization (*Everything ran like clockwork*). It is positive and fits any register; *(as) regular as clockwork* is a common variant.
examples: The dog next door starts barking at six every morning, **like clockwork**.
Thanks to a great wedding planner, the whole day went **like clockwork**.
The new subway line runs **like clockwork**, with a train every four minutes.

drill.sentence: My grandfather calls me every Sunday at noon, {{like clockwork}}, just to ask whether I'm eating enough.
drill.hint: with perfect regularity — a watch image (not *without fail*)

entries.related: *without fail* — every time, with no exceptions; *(as) regular as clockwork* — same idea; *go off without a hitch* — happen smoothly, with no problems.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop doing something while things are going well, before your luck changes and you lose what you have gained.
entries.usage: Mostly given as advice, in the imperative or with *should*: *Quit while you're ahead.* It sounds like advice to a gambler, but it is used about jokes, careers, arguments and sports. The pronoun and tense change (*she quit while she was ahead*); *stop while you're ahead* is a less common variant.
entries.pattern: quit while you're / I'm / they were ahead
examples: I won forty dollars at the slot machines and decided to **quit while I was ahead**.
The show ended after three great seasons; the writers wanted to **quit while they were ahead**.
You got Mom to agree to the sleepover, so **quit while you're ahead** and don't ask for pizza too.

drill.sentence: His first two jokes got big laughs, so I told him to {{quit while he was ahead}} before he tried a third.
drill.hint: stop before his luck turned (not *stop …*)

entries.related: *know when to stop* — plainer; *push your luck* — the opposite, keep taking risks after success; *go out on a high note* — end something at its best moment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very different from something, usually much worse or much better.
entries.usage: Used in speech and writing to compare a situation with an earlier one or with what was expected: *The new apartment is a far cry from our old studio.* It is always followed by *from*. It often means that something falls short (*a far cry from what we were promised*), but it can also show progress.
entries.pattern: be a far cry from + noun / -ing
examples: Our hotel room was **a far cry from** the photos on the website: tiny, dark and noisy.
Today's smartphones are **a far cry from** the brick-sized cell phones of the 1980s.
Coaching a team of six-year-olds is **a far cry from** her years in the pros, but she loves it.

drill.sentence: The salary they offered was {{a far cry from}} the number the recruiter had mentioned on the phone.
drill.hint: very different from — an image of a distant shout (not *nowhere near* or *a long way from*)

entries.related: *nowhere near* — not close to, for amounts and quality; *worlds apart* — completely different; *a long way from* — similar, also used literally.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A small problem or drawback that spoils something that is otherwise good.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, often with *the only* or *one*: *The only fly in the ointment is the price.* It describes a single flaw in a good situation, not a disaster. The form is fixed.
examples: We love the new apartment; the only **fly in the ointment** is the bar downstairs that stays open until 2 a.m.
Rain on the last day was **a fly in the ointment**, but the festival still broke attendance records.
The used car seemed perfect until we found **a fly in the ointment**: the seller still owed money on it.

drill.sentence: The wedding was beautiful; the only {{fly in the ointment}} was the DJ, who played the wrong song for the first dance.
drill.hint: small thing that spoiled it — an insect image (not *snag* or *downside*)

entries.related: *a snag* — a small, unexpected problem; *a catch* — a hidden drawback in an offer; *a downside* — a disadvantage.
entries.origin: From the Bible (Ecclesiastes 10:1), where dead flies spoil a perfumer's ointment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The situation has changed so much that earlier predictions, plans or agreements no longer apply, and anything could happen.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, sports and business news, often after a condition: *If it snows, all bets are off.* It can also mean that an earlier promise or deal no longer holds. The form is fixed, apart from tense (*all bets were off*).
examples: We should get there by noon, but if we hit traffic on the bridge, **all bets are off**.
Once their star quarterback got hurt, **all bets were off** for the playoffs.
I promised to keep your secret, but if you lie to me again, **all bets are off**.

drill.sentence: Our toddler usually naps for two hours, but if she skips lunch, {{all bets are off}}.
drill.hint: nothing can be predicted anymore — a gambling image (not *who knows*)

entries.related: *anything can happen* — plainer; *it's anyone's guess* — nobody knows; *a whole new ball game* — a completely changed situation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To lose your good reputation, status or power, usually suddenly and because of something wrong you did.
entries.usage: Common in news and biographies about celebrities, athletes, executives and companies. It works as a verb (*he fell from grace*) and even more often as a noun (*his fall from grace*), sometimes with *dramatic* or *spectacular*. It sounds serious and a little literary, but it is also used playfully.
entries.pattern: fall from grace / someone's fall from grace
examples: The celebrity chef **fell from grace** after former employees described years of yelling and threats in his kitchens.
Her **fall from grace** was fast: one leaked email, and the board asked her to resign.
Pluto's **fall from grace** came in 2006, when astronomers decided it wasn't a full planet after all.

drill.sentence: The bakery was the most popular spot in town, but it {{fell from grace}} when customers learned it was selling store-bought pies as homemade.
drill.hint: lost its good name — a religious image (not *… out of favor*)

entries.related: *fall out of favor* — become less popular, without disgrace; *a downfall* — a loss of power or success; *disgraced* — the adjective, as in *a disgraced banker*.
entries.origin: From the King James Bible (Galatians 5:4): *ye are fallen from grace*.

entries.term: keep an eye out for something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To watch for someone or something so that you notice them if they appear.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday speech and emails, often as a request: *Keep an eye out for a white van.* It differs from *keep an eye on*, which means to watch over someone or something already in view. *Keep your eyes peeled* is more informal; *keep an eye open for* is also used.
entries.pattern: keep an eye out (for someone / something)
examples: The movers are coming at ten, so **keep an eye out for** a big white truck.
Hikers should **keep an eye out for** rattlesnakes on this trail in the summer.
I'm **keeping an eye out for** a used bike for my daughter, so let me know if you see one.

drill.sentence: Our cat slipped out last night. If you're driving around the neighborhood, please {{keep an eye out for}} a gray tabby.
drill.hint: watch for it to appear (not *look out for*, *be on the lookout for* or *… your eyes peeled for*)

mistake.wrong: Can you keep an eye on a taxi while I get the bags?
mistake.right: Can you keep an eye out for a taxi while I get the bags?
mistake.why: *Keep an eye on* means watching something that is already there; for something you hope will appear, use *keep an eye out for*.

entries.related: *keep an eye on* — watch over, look after; *keep your eyes peeled* — informal, watch carefully; *be on the lookout for* — same meaning, a little more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To think about and discuss a problem as a group, in order to find a solution or make a plan.
entries.usage: Used about two or more people, often as a friendly suggestion: *Let's put our heads together and figure this out.* The possessive matches the subject (*our / their heads*), and *heads* is always plural. It sounds cooperative and fits work, family and community groups.
examples: Let's **put our heads together** after lunch and figure out how to cover the weekend shifts.
The neighbors **put their heads together** and turned the empty lot into a community garden.
If the three of us **put our heads together**, I bet we can plan a surprise party Mom won't see coming.

drill.sentence: We couldn't figure out how to get the couch up the narrow stairs, so the movers {{put their heads together}} and took the door off its hinges.
drill.hint: thought it through as a group (not *brainstormed*)

entries.related: *brainstorm* — produce many ideas quickly in a group; *pool your resources* — combine money or skills; *two heads are better than one* — the proverb behind the idea.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: It is easy to make promises or claims; what really counts is what you actually do.
entries.usage: A skeptical comment in conversation, sports and business, often followed by a demand for action: *Talk is cheap. Show me.* It is a fixed sentence, usually aimed at someone else's promises, and it can sound blunt.
examples: He keeps saying he'll pay me back, but **talk is cheap**.
The airline apologized again for the delays, but **talk is cheap**; passengers want their refunds.
"**Talk is cheap**," Grandma told the contractor. "Show me a finished kitchen."

drill.sentence: My brother says he'll start going to the gym every morning, but {{talk is cheap}}; he said the same thing last January.
drill.hint: promises cost nothing (not *actions speak louder than words* or *easier said than done*)

entries.related: *actions speak louder than words* — what you do matters more than what you say; *put your money where your mouth is* — back up your words with action; *easier said than done* — harder than it sounds.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act as if you are calm, happy or confident when you are actually upset, worried or afraid.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing about hard times such as illness, bad news or a painful loss. It is often followed by *for* + the people you want to protect: *She put on a brave face for the kids.* *Put a brave face on it* and *put up a brave front* are close variants.
entries.pattern: put on a brave face (for someone)
examples: Even after he lost his job, Dad **put on a brave face** for us kids at dinner.
The players **put on a brave face** after the loss, but the locker room was completely silent.
Waving goodbye at the airport, she **put on a brave face**, but she cried all the way home.

drill.sentence: Lena was terrified before her surgery, but she {{put on a brave face}} so her parents wouldn't worry.
drill.hint: hid her fear behind a courageous look (not *kept it together*)

entries.related: *keep a stiff upper lip* — stay calm and hide your feelings, often linked with the British; *keep it together* — stay in control of your emotions; *grin and bear it* — accept something unpleasant without complaining.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person who seems kind, friendly or harmless but actually intends to harm others.
entries.usage: A strong warning or accusation, used in conversation, news and fiction about people, companies or offers. The phrase is fixed: *sheep's clothing*, not *clothes*.
examples: The friendly new neighbor was **a wolf in sheep's clothing**; he'd been stealing packages from every porch on the street.
That zero-interest credit card is **a wolf in sheep's clothing**: the rate jumps to 29 percent after six months.
In the thriller, the sweet babysitter is **a wolf in sheep's clothing**, and the audience realizes it too late.

drill.sentence: Grandma trusted the charming man who offered to fix her roof for half price, but he was {{a wolf in sheep's clothing}} and disappeared with her deposit.
drill.hint: dangerous under a gentle disguise — an animal image (not *a con artist*)

mistake.wrong: He seemed so kind, but he was a wolf in sheep's skin.
mistake.right: He seemed so kind, but he was a wolf in sheep's clothing.
mistake.why: English uses *clothing* here, although German (*Wolf im Schafspelz*) and many other languages say *skin* or *fur*.

entries.related: *two-faced* — friendly to your face but disloyal behind your back; *a snake in the grass* — a hidden enemy, often a false friend; *too good to be true* — about offers that hide a trick.
entries.origin: From the Bible (Matthew 7:15), a warning against false prophets who come *in sheep's clothing*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deliberately ignore someone or treat them in an unfriendly way, usually to show that you are hurt or angry.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about friends, couples, coworkers and classmates: *She's been giving me the cold shoulder since the party.* It describes quiet coldness that the other person clearly notices, not open anger. The person on the receiving end *gets the cold shoulder*.
entries.pattern: give someone the cold shoulder / get the cold shoulder
examples: Ever since I forgot her birthday, my sister has been **giving me the cold shoulder**.
When the new guy joined the team, the older players **gave him the cold shoulder** for weeks.
Lisa **got the cold shoulder** at the reunion from friends she hadn't called in years.

drill.sentence: After I parked in his spot by mistake, my neighbor {{gave me the cold shoulder}} for a whole week.
drill.hint: treated me in an icy, unfriendly way on purpose (not *froze me out* or *… the silent treatment*)

entries.related: *freeze someone out* — exclude someone from a group; *the silent treatment* — refusing to speak to someone; *snub* — one word, ignore someone in a rude way.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have all the advantages and power in a situation, so that you control the outcome.
entries.usage: Common in talk about negotiations, business, relationships and sports, with the stronger side as the subject: *In this market, buyers hold all the cards.* It implies that the other side has little choice. *Hold the cards* and *have all the cards* are also used.
examples: With twenty people applying for one apartment, the landlord **holds all the cards**.
In salary talks, she **held all the cards**: two other companies had already made her offers.
When it comes to bedtime, our three-year-old seems to **hold all the cards**.

drill.sentence: There's only one plumber in our little town, so when your pipes burst on a holiday, he {{holds all the cards}}.
drill.hint: has every advantage — a poker image (not *calls the shots* or *has the upper hand*)

entries.related: *have the upper hand* — have more power or an advantage; *call the shots* — make the decisions; *a bargaining chip* — something you can trade in a negotiation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: For a long period of time, especially when you stay committed despite difficulties.
entries.usage: Common in talk about relationships, careers, investments and projects, typically in *be in it for the long haul*. It stresses commitment and endurance, not just length. *Over the long haul* means *over a long period of time*: *Stocks usually rise over the long haul.*
entries.pattern: (be in it) for the long haul
examples: Buying a house only makes sense if you plan to stay in the area **for the long haul**.
The company is hiring people **for the long haul**, not just for the holiday rush.
Marriage is hard sometimes, but we're in this **for the long haul**.

drill.sentence: Some parrots live for sixty years, so if you adopt one, you have to be in it {{for the long haul}}.
drill.hint: for many years, through good times and bad — a trucking image (not *for life*)

entries.related: *in the long run* — eventually, over a long period; *stick it out* — continue despite difficulties; *a marathon, not a sprint* — a long effort that needs a steady pace.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An effort that is sure to fail, usually because the problem is too big or keeps coming back.
entries.usage: Usually with *fight*: *fight a losing battle against / with something*. It sounds resigned and is often humorous about chores, pests, habits or aging. *It's a losing battle* and *feel like a losing battle* are also common.
entries.pattern: fight a losing battle (against / with something)
examples: With two dogs and a toddler, keeping the floors clean is **a losing battle**.
The small bookstore fought **a losing battle** against online retailers and closed last spring.
Getting teenagers off their phones at dinner can feel like **a losing battle**.

drill.sentence: Every fall, my dad fights {{a losing battle}} against the leaves; the big oak next door drops a fresh layer on our lawn every night.
drill.hint: a fight he can never win (not *an uphill …*)

entries.related: *an uphill battle* — very difficult but still possible; *a lost cause* — something with no hope of success; *spin your wheels* — make an effort without any progress.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Extremely useful or valuable.
entries.usage: Warm, slightly exaggerated praise for people, tools and advice, common in conversation and reviews: *A good babysitter is worth her weight in gold.* The pronoun matches the subject (*its / his / her / their weight*).
entries.pattern: be worth its / his / her / their weight in gold
examples: That advice from my first boss, to always read a contract twice, has been **worth its weight in gold**.
On a long road trip with kids, a tablet full of downloaded movies is **worth its weight in gold**.
Our office manager knows every plumber and electrician in town; she's **worth her weight in gold**.

drill.sentence: When the power went out for three days, our little camping stove was {{worth its weight in gold}}.
drill.hint: extremely valuable — a precious-metal image (not *a lifesaver* or *a godsend*)

entries.related: *priceless* — too valuable to measure; *a lifesaver* — something that helps you in a difficult moment; *a godsend* — something good that arrives exactly when needed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop yourself from saying what you really think, usually to avoid an argument or to avoid hurting someone.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often with *have to*: *I had to bite my tongue.* It implies that you wanted to say something critical or rude. As an exclamation, *Bite your tongue!* is a joking way to tell someone not to say something, such as a bad prediction.
examples: When my mother-in-law criticized my cooking again, I **bit my tongue** and passed the potatoes.
The referee made a terrible call, but the coach **bit his tongue**; one more outburst and he'd be thrown out.
I had to **bite my tongue** in the meeting when my manager presented my idea as his own.

drill.sentence: The flight attendant was rude to me, but I {{bit my tongue}}; arguing at thirty thousand feet never ends well.
drill.hint: stopped myself from snapping back (not *held my …*, *kept quiet* or *kept my mouth shut*)

entries.related: *hold your tongue* — same meaning, a little more formal; *keep your mouth shut* — blunt; *speak your mind* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To accept an opportunity immediately and eagerly.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, often as *would jump at the chance to* + verb: *Most kids would jump at the chance to meet their hero.* *Jump at the opportunity* and *leap at the chance* are common variants. It suggests real enthusiasm, not just agreement.
entries.pattern: jump at the chance (to + verb)
examples: When her company offered her a year in Tokyo, she **jumped at the chance**.
The animal shelter needed foster homes for puppies, and my whole family **jumped at the chance**.
If anyone offered me a free cooking class in Paris, I'd **jump at the chance**.

drill.sentence: When the neighbors asked if we wanted their old piano for free, we {{jumped at the chance}}.
drill.hint: said yes eagerly and right away (not *leaped at …* or *… the offer*)

entries.related: *seize the opportunity* — more formal; *grab the chance* — informal; *pass up a chance* — the opposite, not take it.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An experience or event that marks an important stage in someone's life, especially the move from childhood to adulthood.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and journalism, often humorously for small shared experiences: *Getting lost on the subway is a rite of passage for new New Yorkers.* It is often followed by *for* + a group. The plural is *rites of passage*.
examples: In many American towns, getting your driver's license at sixteen is **a rite of passage**.
Terrible first apartments are **a rite of passage**; everyone has a story about mice or a broken heater.
For new nurses, the first night shift alone is **a rite of passage** they never forget.

drill.sentence: Getting your ears pierced at the mall was {{a rite of passage}} for girls at my middle school.
drill.hint: an experience that marked growing up (not *a milestone*)

mistake.wrong: Getting your first paycheck is a right of passage.
mistake.right: Getting your first paycheck is a rite of passage.
mistake.why: *Rite* means a ceremony; *right of passage* is a very common spelling mistake, even among native speakers.

entries.related: *a milestone* — an important point in progress; *coming of age* — becoming an adult, as in *a coming-of-age story*; *a baptism of fire* — a hard first experience.
entries.origin: From the French *rites de passage*, a term introduced by the anthropologist Arnold van Gennep in 1909.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very varied or disorganized, with no clear focus or pattern.
entries.usage: Informal American English, used about talks, writing, opinions, prices and results: *His presentation was all over the map.* It is critical when it describes thinking or communication, and neutral when it describes a wide spread of numbers or opinions. *All over the place* means the same and is used everywhere.
examples: The meeting was **all over the map**; we talked for an hour and decided nothing.
Prices for the same flight were **all over the map**, from 180 to 600 dollars.
Ask five friends where to eat in Chicago, and the answers will be **all over the map**.

drill.sentence: The detective's theories were {{all over the map}}: first the butler, then the gardener, then a stranger from out of town.
drill.hint: scattered, with no clear focus — the American geography image (not *… the place*)

entries.related: *all over the place* — same meaning, also British; *scattered* — lacking focus; *rambling* — long and unfocused, about speech or writing.

entries.term: the proof is in the pudding
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: You can only judge whether something is good by trying it or seeing the results, not by what people say about it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and business, usually after a claim: *They say the new system is faster, but the proof is in the pudding.* It is a shortened form of an older proverb, so some people find it illogical, but it is now the usual form in American English.
examples: The ads say this mattress will cure your back pain, but **the proof is in the pudding**.
Everyone says the new coach is a genius. Well, **the proof is in the pudding**; let's see how the season goes.
The new screening method sounds clever, but **the proof is in the pudding**: does it catch more cancers than the old one?

drill.sentence: The contractor swears the new roof won't leak, but {{the proof is in the pudding}}; we'll find out when the spring rains come.
drill.hint: you only know by testing it — a dessert image (not *time will tell*)

entries.related: *time will tell* — we will know later; *seeing is believing* — you need to see it yourself; *put something to the test* — try it out.
entries.origin: A shortened form of the 17th-century proverb *the proof of the pudding is in the eating*, where *proof* meant *test*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To suddenly announce something shocking or very surprising, usually news that changes the situation.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news. Typical frames are *drop a bombshell (on someone)* and *drop the bombshell that …*. The news is usually unwelcome or dramatic and comes without warning; *bombshell* alone also works as a noun: *The report was a bombshell.*
entries.pattern: drop a bombshell (on someone) / drop the bombshell that …
examples: Halfway through Thanksgiving dinner, my brother **dropped a bombshell**: he and his wife were moving to Australia.
The company **dropped a bombshell** on Friday afternoon, announcing that the factory would close in March.
My best friend **dropped the bombshell** that she was quitting med school to become a pastry chef.

drill.sentence: In the last episode, the narrator {{dropped a bombshell}}: she had been the killer all along.
drill.hint: suddenly revealed something shocking — an explosive image (not *broke the news*)

entries.related: *break the news* — tell someone bad news, often gently; *a bolt from the blue* — a complete surprise; *drop a hint* — suggest something indirectly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start believing that something good will happen, often when it probably won't.
entries.usage: Usually negative, as a warning: *Don't get your hopes up.* It is common in everyday talk about jobs, dates, test results and sports. The possessive changes, and *get someone's hopes up* means making someone else hopeful, often unfairly.
examples: I applied for the job at the museum, but I'm trying not to **get my hopes up**.
Please don't mention the beach trip to the kids yet; I don't want to **get their hopes up**.
Fans **got their hopes up** after five straight wins, and then the team lost the next ten.

drill.sentence: The doctor said the new treatment might help, but she warned us not to {{get our hopes up}} too much.
drill.hint: become too optimistic (not *count on it*)

entries.related: *count your chickens before they hatch* — expect success too early; *don't hold your breath* — don't expect it soon; *dash someone's hopes* — destroy them.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do bad or annoying things without being punished or criticized, usually because someone lets you.
entries.usage: Informal and exaggerated: it describes everyday misbehavior, not real crime. It is common about children, pets, favorite employees and star players, and it often suggests unfair favoritism. The form is fixed except for tense: *He gets / got away with murder.*
examples: My little brother **gets away with murder**; if I'd talked to Mom like that, I'd have been grounded for a month.
Because he's the boss's nephew, he **gets away with murder** at the office.
Our cat **gets away with murder**: she sleeps on the kitchen counter and nobody says a word.

drill.sentence: At their grandparents' house, the kids stay up late and eat candy for dinner; they {{get away with murder}} there.
drill.hint: behave badly with no punishment at all — an exaggerated crime image (not *do as they please*)

entries.related: *get away with something* — avoid punishment for one specific thing; *get off scot-free* — escape punishment completely; *a slap on the wrist* — a very light punishment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To avoid giving someone a clear answer or the help they need, often by sending them from one person or excuse to another.
entries.usage: Common in complaints about companies, offices, landlords and partners: *The insurance company keeps giving me the runaround.* The person on the receiving end *gets the runaround*. American English writes it as one word: *runaround*.
entries.pattern: give someone the runaround / get the runaround
examples: I've called the insurance company six times, and they keep **giving me the runaround**.
Ask the city about the pothole on our street, and you'll **get the runaround**: every office says it's someone else's job.
Every time Jen asks her boyfriend about moving in together, he **gives her the runaround**.

drill.sentence: Instead of telling me when my car would be ready, the repair shop {{gave me the runaround}} for two weeks.
drill.hint: kept dodging a clear answer (not *strung me along* or *jerked me around*)

entries.related: *string someone along* — keep someone hoping without meaning to deliver; *pass the buck* — shift responsibility to someone else; *stonewall* — refuse to answer at all.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Fiercely competitive, with people ready to harm others in order to succeed.
entries.usage: Used about industries, cities, schools and the world in general, typically in *a dog-eat-dog world / business* or *It's dog-eat-dog out there*. It sounds cynical or resigned. It is written with hyphens.
entries.pattern: a dog-eat-dog world / business; it's dog-eat-dog (out there)
examples: College sports recruiting is **dog-eat-dog**; coaches will promise almost anything to sign a top player.
"It's a **dog-eat-dog** world out there," Dad said when I complained about my first job.
Competition for spots in the youth orchestra has become **dog-eat-dog**, with parents hiring private coaches for six-year-olds.

drill.sentence: The restaurant business in New York is {{dog-eat-dog}}: half the new places close within a year.
drill.hint: ruthlessly competitive — an animal image (not *cutthroat*)

entries.related: *cutthroat* — ruthless in competition; *the rat race* — the exhausting competition of working life; *every man for himself* — everyone looks after only themselves.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Wait a moment; slow down and don't act or decide too quickly.
entries.usage: Informal and playful, said as a command to someone who is rushing ahead or getting too excited: *Hold your horses! We haven't agreed yet.* It sounds a little old-fashioned and folksy, is used almost only in the imperative, and can seem bossy if you say it to a superior.
examples: **Hold your horses**! We're not opening presents until Grandma gets here.
"Let's book the flights tonight!" "**Hold your horses**; I don't even know if I can get time off."
Before you quit your job to sell candles online, **hold your horses** and talk to someone who's done it.

drill.sentence: "I'm going to post our engagement photos right now!" "{{Hold your horses}}! Let's tell our parents first."
drill.hint: wait, don't rush — a riding image (not *slow down*, *wait a minute* or *not so fast*)

entries.related: *not so fast* — a firmer warning; *slow down* — plainer; *jump the gun* — act too soon.

entries.term: give someone a run for their money
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To compete so well against someone that they have to try very hard to win.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and everyday comparisons, and usually admiring, often about a smaller or newer rival: *The new pizza place is giving Tony's a run for its money.* The possessive matches the person or thing being challenged (*their / his / its money*).
entries.pattern: give someone a run for their money
examples: Nobody expected much from the small-town team, but they **gave the champions a run for their money**.
My eight-year-old **gives me a run for my money** at chess these days.
The new taco truck by the park is **giving the old diner a run for its money**.

drill.sentence: She's only been playing tennis for a year, but she {{gave her coach a run for his money}} in their last match.
drill.hint: made him work hard to win (not *pushed him to the limit*)

entries.related: *hold your own* — perform well against stronger opponents; *neck and neck* — exactly level in a race; *outclass* — be much better than someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Completely different from each other, often about a change from before to after.
entries.usage: Informal, used to compare two people, things or situations: *My two kids are like night and day.* Common frames are *be like night and day* and *the difference is (like) night and day*; *a night-and-day difference* is also common. *Like day and night* is also used.
examples: My twins are **like night and day**: one never stops talking, and the other barely says a word.
The difference in my energy since I cut out sugar is **like night and day**.
Switching from my ten-year-old laptop to a new one was **like night and day**.

drill.sentence: Moving to a small town after ten years in Chicago was {{like night and day}}; I could actually hear birds in the morning.
drill.hint: a total contrast — a time-of-day image (not *a whole different world*)

entries.related: *worlds apart* — very different; *chalk and cheese* — the British equivalent; *apples and oranges* — too different to compare fairly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To solve a problem or achieve the result you need.
entries.usage: Very common and informal, used about simple fixes, remedies and small actions: *A little salt should do the trick.* The subject is usually a thing or an action, rarely a person. It often appears with *should* or *that'll*: *That'll do the trick.*
examples: If the cake is too dry, a little warm syrup on top should **do the trick**.
I tried everything for my hiccups, and in the end, a spoonful of sugar **did the trick**.
Restarting the router **did the trick**, and the Wi-Fi came back.

drill.sentence: My new jeans were too long, but a quick visit to the tailor {{did the trick}}.
drill.hint: solved the problem — a magic image (not *did the job*)

entries.related: *do the job* — same meaning, plainer; *work like a charm* — work perfectly; *hit the spot* — about food or drink, satisfy exactly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A point in life or in a process where you must choose between two or more different directions.
entries.usage: Used about careers, relationships and big decisions, often with *come to*, *reach* or *be at*: *We've reached a fork in the road.* It sounds reflective and is common in interviews, speeches and personal stories. It is also used literally for a place where a road splits.
examples: After graduation, I came to **a fork in the road**: take the job in Seattle or stay near my family.
The band reached **a fork in the road** when the lead singer was offered a solo deal.
Retirement is **a fork in the road** for many couples, who suddenly have to decide where and how to live.

drill.sentence: At forty, Maria found herself at {{a fork in the road}}: keep teaching or go back to school to become a nurse.
drill.hint: a moment of big choice between two paths (not *a crossroads*)

entries.related: *at a crossroads* — same meaning, a little more formal; *a turning point* — a moment of important change; *the point of no return* — after it, you cannot go back.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To cause trouble or disturb a calm situation, usually by complaining, criticizing or challenging how things are done.
entries.usage: Very often in the negative: *I don't want to make waves.* It describes people who keep quiet to avoid conflict, or who bravely refuse to. In a different, positive sense, *making waves* can also mean attracting a lot of attention, as in *a young chef making waves in the city*.
examples: I didn't like the new schedule, but I'd just started, so I didn't want to **make waves**.
Our neighbor **made waves** at the homeowners' meeting by asking where all the fees were going.
Good nurses sometimes have to **make waves** when they see a patient being ignored.

drill.sentence: My aunt never sends food back at restaurants, even when it's cold; she hates to {{make waves}}.
drill.hint: cause trouble or a fuss (not *rock the boat* or *… a scene*)

entries.related: *rock the boat* — same meaning, very common; *stir the pot* — cause trouble on purpose; *make a splash* — attract a lot of attention.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To treat something serious as if it were unimportant or funny.
entries.usage: Used in speech and writing, often critically: *You shouldn't make light of his illness.* The negative *I don't mean to make light of …* is a common polite way to soften a joke or a hopeful remark. It can also be kind or brave, when people make light of their own pain.
entries.pattern: make light of + noun
examples: I don't mean to **make light of** your problem, but honestly, it could have been much worse.
He **made light of** his broken arm, joking that he finally had an excuse to skip yard work.
The comedian was criticized for **making light of** a flood that destroyed hundreds of homes.

drill.sentence: My brother {{made light of}} his car accident, but we could tell he was still shaken weeks later.
drill.hint: treated it as nothing serious (not *laughed off* or *played down*)

entries.related: *play down* — make something seem less important; *laugh something off* — joke about it to show it doesn't matter; *take something seriously* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Having information, often private or insider information, that most people don't have.
entries.usage: Informal, common in conversation, journalism and travel or food writing: *People in the know say the store is closing.* Typical frames are *those / people in the know* and *be in the know about something*. It can sound slightly exclusive or trendy.
examples: People **in the know** say the old mall will be torn down next year.
If you want to be **in the know** about school events, join the parents' group chat.
Anyone **in the know** books a table two weeks ahead; walk-ins wait for hours.

drill.sentence: My neighbor works at city hall, so she's always {{in the know}} when a new restaurant is about to open.
drill.hint: has inside information before others (not *in the loop*)

entries.related: *in the loop* — kept informed, especially at work; *an insider* — someone with inside information; *out of the loop* — not informed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To worry a lot about something.
entries.usage: Usually in the negative, to say that something isn't worth worrying about: *Don't lose any sleep over it.* *I'm not losing any sleep over it* can sound relaxed or a little dismissive. In the positive, it describes real, ongoing worry.
entries.pattern: (not) lose (any) sleep over something
examples: It's one bad online review of your bakery; I wouldn't **lose any sleep over** it.
He's been **losing sleep over** whether to take the job in Denver.
Plenty of parents **lose sleep over** their teenagers' driving.

drill.sentence: The scratch on the car is tiny, and the insurance will cover it, so don't {{lose sleep over}} it.
drill.hint: be anxious about — a bedtime image (not *worry about* or *stress over*)

entries.related: *worry yourself sick* — worry very much; *keep someone up at night* — make someone worry; *not give it a second thought* — not worry at all.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To lie openly and shamelessly, knowing that what you say is completely false.
entries.usage: Informal and usually critical, common in conversation and news about salespeople, witnesses and cheating partners: *He's lying through his teeth.* People also use it humorously about their own polite lies. The possessive matches the subject (*through his / her / their teeth*), and it is very often in the progressive.
examples: The used-car salesman was **lying through his teeth** when he said the car had never been in an accident.
I told my aunt I loved her fruitcake, but I was **lying through my teeth**.
The witness **lied through her teeth** on the stand, and the jury didn't believe a word.

drill.sentence: My roommate looked me in the eye and swore he'd paid the electric bill, but he was {{lying through his teeth}}.
drill.hint: telling a total falsehood shamelessly — a mouth image (not *flat-out …*)

entries.related: *a barefaced lie* — an obvious, shameless lie; *a white lie* — a small, harmless lie; *flat-out lie* — informal, say something completely false.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To forgive someone for something in the past and forget about it, so that the relationship can continue.
entries.usage: Used to suggest making peace after an argument or a long feud: *Let's let bygones be bygones.* The form is fixed and sounds warm and a little old-fashioned. *Bygones* means past events, and the word is rarely used outside this phrase.
examples: My uncle and my dad hadn't spoken in ten years, but at Grandma's ninetieth birthday, they decided to **let bygones be bygones**.
The two former rivals **let bygones be bygones** and now host a podcast together.
"Are you still mad about the wedding?" "No. Let's just **let bygones be bygones**."

drill.sentence: We had a big fight over money years ago, but she called me last week, and we agreed to {{let bygones be bygones}}.
drill.hint: leave the old quarrel in the past (not *bury the hatchet* or *forgive and forget*)

entries.related: *bury the hatchet* — make peace after a conflict; *water under the bridge* — something in the past that no longer matters; *hold a grudge* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To become noticed and successful, so that people recognize your influence or achievement.
entries.usage: Common in talk about careers, sports and the arts. Typical patterns are *make your mark as* + role, *make your mark in* + field and *make your mark on* + place or thing. It sounds positive and a little formal, typical of profiles, speeches and graduation talks.
entries.pattern: make your mark (as / in / on …)
examples: She **made her mark** as a chef in Chicago before opening her own restaurant in Austin.
The rookie **made his mark** in his very first game, scoring two goals.
Every generation of architects wants to **make its mark on** the city skyline.

drill.sentence: Within two years of joining the newspaper, the young reporter had {{made her mark}} with a series on unsafe bridges.
drill.hint: got noticed for her achievements (not *… a name for herself* or *… it big*)

entries.related: *make a name for yourself* — become well known; *leave your mark* — have a lasting influence; *make it big* — become very successful.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Unique; unlike anyone or anything else.
entries.usage: Common, warm praise for people, objects and places: *She's one of a kind.* Before a noun it takes hyphens: *a one-of-a-kind dress*. In ads and shops it often means handmade, or the only one made.
examples: My grandfather was **one of a kind**: a farmer, a jazz pianist and the best storyteller in town.
She wore a **one-of-a-kind** dress that her aunt had sewn by hand.
The tiny hotel, built inside an old fire station, is truly **one of a kind**.

drill.sentence: There was nobody like our old music teacher; she was truly {{one of a kind}}.
drill.hint: unlike anyone else (not *unique* or *one in a million*)

entries.related: *one in a million* — exceptionally rare and good, about people; *unique* — the plain word; *a one-off* — British, something done or made only once.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A problem or difficulty that stops progress or prevents an agreement.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and negotiations, neutral to slightly formal: *Price remains the main stumbling block.* Typical frames are *the main / biggest stumbling block*, *a stumbling block to* + noun and *a stumbling block for* + person.
examples: We'd love to move to the coast; the biggest **stumbling block** is finding jobs there for both of us.
For many adult learners, irregular verbs are the first real **stumbling block**.
Talks between the teachers and the school district broke down, with health insurance the main **stumbling block**.

drill.sentence: The sale of the house almost fell through; the main {{stumbling block}} was a crack in the foundation.
drill.hint: the problem that held everything up (not *sticking point*, *hurdle* or *obstacle*)

entries.related: *a sticking point* — an issue that people cannot agree on; *an obstacle* — the general word; *a roadblock* — informal, something that stops progress completely.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In an uncertain situation where you are waiting for a decision and cannot move forward.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news about plans, legal cases, projects and careers. Typical verbs are *be*, *remain*, *leave* and *hang*: *The delay left hundreds of families in limbo.* It suggests frustration with a delay that someone else controls.
examples: My transfer request has been **in limbo** for months, so I can't sign a new lease.
Hundreds of workers were left **in limbo** when the factory's new owners delayed their decision on layoffs.
The movie sat **in limbo** for three years after the studio was sold.

drill.sentence: Our wedding plans are {{in limbo}} until we know whether the venue will reopen after the fire.
drill.hint: stuck, waiting for a decision (not *on hold* or *up in the air*)

entries.related: *up in the air* — not yet decided; *on hold* — paused; *in a holding pattern* — waiting and unable to move forward, from aviation.
entries.origin: From Latin *limbus* ('edge'): in medieval Christian theology, Limbo was a region at the edge of hell for souls kept out of heaven through no fault of their own.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A process in which something small grows bigger and faster, because each result adds to the next.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and everyday talk, usually with *have*, *create* or *start*: *One late payment can have a snowball effect.* It works for good things (savings, popularity) and bad things (debt, rumors). The verb is also common: *The problem snowballed.*
examples: One missed payment started **a snowball effect**: late fees, a lower credit score and higher interest rates.
When a famous chef praised the little taco stand, it created **a snowball effect**, and soon the line went around the block.
A single rumor about the school closing had **a snowball effect**; by Friday, parents were pulling their kids out.

drill.sentence: Once a few neighbors put solar panels on their roofs, there was {{a snowball effect}}, and soon half the street had them.
drill.hint: a process that kept growing bigger and faster — a winter image (not the *domino* or *ripple* kind)

entries.related: *a domino effect* — one event causes a chain of similar events; *a ripple effect* — effects that spread outward; *a vicious circle* — problems that keep causing each other.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said to show that you will never allow something to happen as long as you can prevent it.
entries.usage: Informal, emphatic and often humorous, usually a short reply to a request, such as a teenager asking for a tattoo. It can also end a sentence: *They'll sell this house over my dead body.* It sounds dramatic, so it suits family arguments and jokes better than work.
examples: "Can I get a motorcycle for my sixteenth birthday?" "**Over my dead body**."
Grandma says she'll move into a nursing home **over her dead body**.
They want to cut down the old oak in front of the library? **Over my dead body**.

drill.sentence: "Dad, can we paint the living room bright purple?" "{{Over my dead body}}! It took me a month to choose this beige."
drill.hint: absolutely never — a dramatic, morbid refusal (not *no way* or *not in a million years*)

entries.related: *not in a million years* — never; *no way* — an informal refusal; *when pigs fly* — it will never happen.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: So new or advanced that people at the time did not fully understand or appreciate it.
entries.usage: Used about ideas, inventions, designs, artists and products, often to explain why something failed or was ignored at first. The possessive matches the subject (*ahead of his / her / their time*). It is usually admiring and often said in hindsight.
examples: The show was canceled after one season, but critics now say it was **ahead of its time**.
My grandmother was **ahead of her time**; she started her own business in 1962, when few women did.
Early video phones were **ahead of their time**; nobody wanted to be seen at home in pajamas.

drill.sentence: When the restaurant opened in 1995, nobody wanted to pay for organic kale salads; it was simply {{ahead of its time}}.
drill.hint: too new for people back then (not *before …*)

entries.related: *before its time* — similar; *cutting-edge* — the most advanced; *behind the times* — the opposite, old-fashioned.

entries.term: your guess is as good as mine
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: I don't know the answer any more than you do.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in conversation, used as a complete reply to a question nobody present can answer. It can sound friendly and shrugging, or a little frustrated when someone else should know the answer, such as an airline or a city office.
examples: "Why is the line at the DMV so long today?" "**Your guess is as good as mine**."
"What's in this casserole?" "Honestly, **your guess is as good as mine**; Aunt Carol made it."
The instructions are all in Swedish, so **your guess is as good as mine**.

drill.sentence: "Why did the game get delayed?" "{{Your guess is as good as mine}}; nobody has announced anything."
drill.hint: I have no more idea than you (not *beats me* or *who knows*)

entries.related: *beats me* — very informal, I don't know; *who knows?* — nobody can know; *it's anyone's guess* — nobody can know for sure.
